section.title: The Canaanite Woman and the Four Thousand
section.sectionRationale: Right after teaching that defilement is of the heart, Jesus crosses into Gentile territory. A Canaanite woman's persistent, humble faith wins a healing for her daughter, and then Jesus feeds four thousand on a Gentile-leaning shore. The gospel is beginning to reach beyond Israel.
section.thesis: The bread of the children is not so scarce that the dogs cannot be fed too: a Gentile woman's great faith and a second feeding on the far shore reveal that the mercy of Israel's Messiah overflows to the nations.
section.frameNote: Two scenes: the faith of the Canaanite woman, whose daughter is healed; and the feeding of the four thousand, an abundance of bread for the crowds.

verses.text: Leaving that place, Jesus withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon.
And a Canaanite woman from that region came to Him, crying out, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me! My daughter is miserably possessed by a demon.”
But Jesus did not answer a word. So His disciples came and urged Him, “Send her away, for she keeps crying out after us.”
He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”
The woman came and knelt before Him. “Lord, help me!” she said.
But Jesus replied, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the {{kynarion|dogs}}.”
“Yes, Lord,” she said, “even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master’s table.”
“O woman,” Jesus answered, “your {{pistis|faith}} is great! Let it be done for you as you desire.” And her daughter was healed from that very hour.

units.label: The feeding of the four thousand

verses.text: Moving on from there, Jesus went along the Sea of Galilee. Then He went up on a mountain and sat down.
Large crowds came to Him, bringing the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and laid them at His feet, and He healed them.
The crowd was amazed when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled restored, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel.

Then Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, “I have {{splanchnizomai|compassion}} for this crowd, because they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat. I do not want to send them away hungry, or they may faint along the way.”
The disciples replied, “Where in this desolate place could we find enough bread to feed such a large crowd?”
“How many loaves do you have?” Jesus asked. “Seven,” they replied, “and a few small fish.”
And He instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground.
Taking the seven loaves and the fish, He gave thanks and broke them. Then He gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people.
They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.
A total of four thousand men were fed, besides women and children.
After Jesus had dismissed the crowds, He got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.

kynarion.gloss: A little dog, a household pet rather than a street scavenger. Jesus' word is gentler than the usual term for dog, and the woman seizes on it: even the little dogs under the table eat the children's crumbs. It frames Israel's priority without slamming the door on the nations.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust, reliance. Jesus commends the woman's faith as great, a rare praise in Matthew, given not to a Jewish leader but to a Gentile woman who clings to His mercy despite every obstacle.

splanchnizomai.gloss: To be moved with compassion from the depths, literally a stirring in the inward parts. It is Jesus' visceral mercy for the hungry crowd, the same compassion that drives His healing and feeding throughout the Gospel.

basic.context: Jesus leaves Jewish territory and enters the region of Tyre and Sidon. A Canaanite woman begs Him to heal her demon-tormented daughter. He seems to refuse, testing her, and she answers with humble, persistent faith: even the little dogs eat the crumbs. Jesus praises her great faith and heals her daughter. Then, on a mountain by the sea, He heals many and feeds a crowd of four thousand with seven loaves and a few fish, with baskets left over.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the woman's story as a test that draws out and displays her faith, not as a cold rejection. Notice the movement of the chapter: from clean and unclean, to a Gentile woman, to a feeding on Gentile-leaning ground. The theme is the mercy of Israel's Messiah beginning to overflow to the nations, even before the Great Commission.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus uses the softer word kynarion, little household dogs, not wild curs, and the woman turns it into an argument for grace. Jesus calls her pistis, her faith, great. At the feeding He is moved with splanchnizomai, gut-deep compassion, for the hungry crowd.
basic.typology: Jesus feeding the multitude in a desolate place echoes God feeding Israel with manna in the wilderness. The abundance, with baskets left over, shows Him as the true bread who satisfies, and the second feeding, reaching toward the Gentiles, foreshadows a table set for all nations.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Son of David whose mercy cannot be confined to Israel. He tests and honors faith, He heals the broken, and He feeds the hungry from His own hand. He is the bread of life, and the crumbs from His table are enough to save.
basic.god: God's plan runs to Israel first and then to the nations. He is not stingy: the children's bread is so abundant that the dogs are fed too. He delights in humble, persistent faith and answers it, and He is glorified as the God of Israel by a Gentile crowd.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 1:16 speaks of the gospel to the Jew first and also to the Greek. Matthew 8 shows another Gentile, the centurion, whose faith Jesus marvels at. Isaiah 25 and 56 promise a feast and a house of prayer for all nations. The manna of Exodus 16 stands behind the feeding.
basic.oneStory: Between His teaching on the heart and His journey to the cross, Jesus lets the mercy of the kingdom spill over Israel's borders. A Gentile woman's faith and a second feeding announce quietly what the risen Christ will command openly: this bread is for the nations, and whoever comes in faith will be filled.

context.literary:
The passage has two panels joined by a change of place. The first, verses 21 to 28, is a tightly drawn dialogue with a rising and falling rhythm. The woman speaks, Jesus is silent; the disciples speak, Jesus answers them rather than her; she speaks again and is met with a hard saying; she answers once more and is granted everything. Three appeals from her, three kinds of resistance from Him, and then the verdict in verse 28. Matthew builds it so that the reader feels the delay before the release.

The second panel, verses 29 to 39, is a summary of healing and then a feeding told at a slower pace. The pattern of the feeding mirrors chapter 14: compassion, a shortage, a count of loaves, a blessing, a breaking, a distribution through the disciples, a surplus, a head count. The differences are deliberate. The crowd has stayed three days, the loaves are seven, the baskets are seven, and the count is four thousand. Matthew keeps both feedings in the reader's mind, and Jesus Himself will later recall them side by side, Matthew 16:9 and 10.

The two panels share a word: bread. The woman asks for crumbs from the children's bread, verses 26 and 27, and Jesus then puts bread in the hands of a crowd. Her request for a crumb is answered by a feast, so the second panel reads as the larger fulfilment of the first. They also share a scene change: the first is in a foreign region, the second on the shore of Galilee where the crowd glorified the God of Israel, verse 31.

In Matthew's argument the passage follows the quarrel over clean and unclean in verses 1 to 20, and it shows what that teaching makes possible: a Gentile can approach without having first to pass through a purity code.
context.historical:
Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician cities on the Mediterranean coast, north of Galilee. They had a long, tangled history with Israel. Sidon is named in the table of nations as the firstborn of Canaan, Genesis 10:15, and Tyre had been a supplier and partner in Solomon's day. Prophets announced judgment on both, and Jesus Himself placed them beside Chorazin and Bethsaida, saying they would have repented if they had seen what Galilee saw, Matthew 11:21 and 22.

Matthew calls the woman a Canaanite, a very old name for the pre-Israelite people of the land, which Mark replaces with 'Greek' and 'Syrophoenician', Mark 7:26, for readers familiar with the Roman province. Matthew's choice evokes Israel's original conflict with the peoples of Canaan, so he makes the most distant outsider the one who comes to Jesus. She was female and non-Jewish, in a society that expected little from either.

The economic ties between the regions matter. Galilee and the Phoenician coast were close neighbors, and Acts 12:20 says Tyre and Sidon depended on the king's country for food. The idea of Gentiles needing the bread of Israel was familiar. The word 'dogs' was a common Jewish way to refer to Gentiles, though the diminutive Jesus uses points to household dogs under the table rather than strays.

The feeding takes place after a trip around the north and the east of the lake. Matthew does not say the crowd is Gentile, but the phrase that they 'glorified the God of Israel', verse 31, sounds like people who had not always done so. The place name in verse 39 differs in the manuscripts, which should make us cautious about a precise location. What is certain is that this is a feeding in a desolate place, and that the disciples again cannot imagine where the food will come from.
context.canonical:
The woman's story depends on a pattern that runs through the Old Testament: God's mercy repeatedly reaches foreigners while Israel is slow to see it. Elijah was sent to the widow of Zarephath in Sidon, 1 Kings 17:8 and 9, and Jesus later points to that story to show that God's favor is not owned by Israel, Luke 4:25 and 26. The very land where she lived was the land where an earlier prophet found bread for a hungry woman and raised her son.

The promises to Abraham are in the background as well: in him all the families of the earth were to be blessed, Genesis 12:3. Isaiah saw foreigners joining themselves to the LORD and being brought to the holy mountain, so that God's house would be called a house of prayer for all nations, Isaiah 56:6 and 7. Isaiah 25:6 to 8 pictures a banquet for all peoples, and the feeding on the mountain gives a foretaste.

Within Matthew, the woman echoes the centurion, whose faith Jesus said He had not found in Israel and who would be joined by many from east and west at the banquet of the kingdom, Matthew 8:10 to 12. The title she uses, Son of David, belongs to Matthew's central claims, as in the cries of the blind men, Matthew 9:27 and 20:30 and 31. Matthew 12:21 had already said that in His name the nations will put their hope.

Beyond the Gospel, Paul sums the pattern in Romans 15:8 and 9: Christ became a servant to the circumcised to confirm the promises, so that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy. Ephesians 2 describes the outcome as strangers brought near. Each of these takes up what is begun in the district of Tyre and Sidon.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wants his readers to see that the mercy of the Messiah, though promised first to Israel, is not rationed. He tells the woman's story with a precision that keeps both truths in sight. Jesus really was sent to the lost sheep of Israel, verse 24, and His mission has an order. Yet that order does not close the door, and the person who comes in humble faith finds it open.

He also means the story as an example of faith. The woman has no claim on Jesus by birth or by merit; she calls on Him as Lord and Son of David, kneels, and keeps asking. When He answers with a hard saying she does not argue her case, she accepts the place He gives her and finds room in it. That is the faith Matthew commends: it receives the terms God sets and trusts His goodness within them.

The feeding of the four thousand has a different job. It reminds readers that the disciples, who see the second feeding as clearly as the first, are still slow to trust. Their question in verse 33, where could we find enough bread, repeats their question in chapter 14 as if the earlier miracle had not happened. Matthew records it so that his readers will not repeat it. In the next chapter Jesus rebukes them for exactly this lapse, Matthew 16:8 to 10.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage narrates how Jesus dealt with one woman; it does not set a rule that every petition must be delayed or that every prayer needs to be met with silence first. Jesus' silence and His hard saying belong to this encounter, in which He is drawing out and showing a faith that others will see. The abiding application is rather that persistent, humble prayer is welcome, as in Luke 18:1 to 8, and that those who feel outside need not stay away.

The word 'dogs' needs care. It describes Jewish usage of the day and Jesus' framing of the salvation-historical order; it does not endorse contempt for any people, and Jesus' own praise of the woman at the end shows where His heart lay. Readers should not use verse 26 to justify any hierarchy among people. The same applies to verse 24: it describes the order of Jesus' earthly mission, and it is lifted at the Great Commission, Matthew 28:19.

The feeding is similarly descriptive. It records what Jesus did for hungry people, not a promise that God will multiply resources whenever believers are short. It does, however, show His compassion for physical need and His practice of working through the disciples' hands, which the church reads as a pattern for service.

debates.question: Why does Jesus answer the woman as He does?

views.label: He is testing her to bring out her faith
views.case: The delay, the silence and the saying about the dogs set up a trial in which her answer shines, and the story ends with His public praise. His eventual 'let it be done for you as you desire' shows that His purpose was to display her faith and not to refuse her.

views.label: He is stating the order of His mission
views.case: He says plainly that He was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, verse 24, and the saying about children's bread restates a priority of salvation history. On this reading the woman earns no exception; she shows that the order is not exclusion, and her faith finds the grace inside it.

views.label: He is speaking for the disciples' benefit
views.case: Some see a teaching moment in which He voices the attitudes of His disciples and Israel so that her reply can correct them. The disciples have just asked that she be sent away, verse 23, and the lesson lands on them as much as on her.

debates.bearing: These views are compatible, and Matthew's own telling supports more than one. What is clear is that the story ends with grace to a Gentile, and that her faith, which comes by nothing but trust, is what He names.

debates.question: Do the numbers, seven loaves and seven baskets, carry meaning?

views.label: Yes, seven suggests completeness and the nations
views.case: The first feeding ends with twelve baskets, an apparent echo of the tribes, and the second with seven, which some link to the seventy nations of Genesis 10 or to completeness. Jesus' recollection of both, Matthew 16:9 and 10, suggests the details were worth remembering.

views.label: No, they are simply the facts of the event
views.case: Matthew gives no explanation of the numbers and Jesus does not interpret them; the text stresses compassion, provision and surplus. Reading hidden codes risks allegory that the passage does not require.

debates.bearing: The safer path is to take the surplus itself as the point, since the Gospel stresses it twice. A Gentile reading is likely but not provable, and the feeding stands as a sign of abundance either way.

study.originalLanguages:
The woman begins with 'Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me', verse 22, and the verb 'crying out' is an imperfect, ekrazen, a cry kept up over time and not a single call. The disciples complain in verse 23 that she 'keeps crying out after us', which is exactly the persistence Matthew describes. Her title for Jesus, kyrie, is the same word she uses in verses 25 and 27, and Matthew has her use it every time. It can mean 'sir', but in this Gospel it grows in weight, and here it carries more than politeness.

Matthew says Jesus 'did not answer a word', verse 23, a phrase in which logos is the word withheld, though in this story the word is also what He finally gives and honors. In verse 24 He says He 'was sent', apestalen, a passive that implies the sender. His mission is received from the Father, and so is its order.

Her gesture in verse 25 is described with proskyneo, usually translated 'knelt' or 'worshiped'. Matthew uses the same verb of the magi, Matthew 2:11, and of the disciples in the boat, Matthew 14:33. Whatever else she understands, she approaches Him with the posture owed to God. The word for the 'children's bread' sets artos, bread, beside teknon, children, a household picture of a family meal. Her reply opens with a particle sequence that can be read as 'Yes, Lord, for even...', agreeing with His premise and then using it. She accepts the order and adds that even dogs are fed at the table.

In verse 28 the imperative is genetheto, 'let it be done', from ginomai, and it echoes what Jesus said to the centurion in Matthew 8:13. The word for 'desire' in 'as you desire' is thelo, to will, so He gives her what she wills. The healing is said to occur 'from that very hour', apo tes horas ekeines.

In the feeding, the gesture of giving thanks in verse 36 is eucharisteo, where the first feeding in Matthew 14:19 used the verb for blessing, eulogeo. Both feedings also differ in the baskets: the word in 14:20 is kophinos, a small hand basket, and in 15:37 it is spyris, a larger basket of the kind in which Paul was lowered over a wall, Acts 9:25. Jesus keeps the two words apart when He recalls the miracles in Matthew 16:9 and 10, which shows how carefully the account was remembered.

typology.type: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, 1 Kings 17:8 to 24
typology.fulfillment: Elijah, the great prophet of Israel, was sent to a widow in the territory of Sidon, where her flour and oil lasted and her dead son was raised. Jesus comes to the same coast, and a Gentile mother again receives life for her child. The correspondence is that God's mercy crosses the border to a woman in need. The escalation is that the One who comes is greater than Elijah and does not need to be sent a long way: the healing happens at a distance by His word, verse 28. The type falls short because Elijah's miracles were gifts through a servant, and Jesus' are His own, Luke 4:25 and 26.

God fed Israel with bread from heaven in a desolate place and tested them as He did so, Exodus 16:4. Jesus feeds a crowd in a desolate place, verse 33, from almost nothing, and everyone is satisfied. Deuteronomy 8:3 says that man lives by every word from the mouth of the LORD, and Jesus later calls Himself the bread of life, John 6:35. The escalation is that the provider is present in person and the bread is given by hand. The type falls short because manna was enough for a day and could not be kept, while Jesus gives life that lasts, John 6:49 and 50.

typology.type: Elisha and the barley loaves, 2 Kings 4:42 to 44
typology.fulfillment: Elisha fed a hundred men from twenty loaves, with food left over according to the word of the LORD. His servant doubted, 'How am I to set twenty loaves before a hundred men?', and the Gospel disciples ask a similar question. The correspondence is multiplication with leftovers and an objecting attendant. The escalation is one of scale and authority: thousands, a few loaves, and Jesus acts in His own name. The type falls short because Elisha spoke the LORD's word while Jesus gives thanks and breaks the bread as the Lord.

typology.type: The banquet on the mountain, Isaiah 25:6 to 8
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah foresaw a feast for all peoples on the LORD's mountain, where death is swallowed up and tears wiped away. The feeding on a mountain by the sea, verses 29 to 38, to a crowd who have come from far and glorify the God of Israel, is a small sign of that day. The healed lame, blind and mute in verse 30 foreshadow the end of suffering. The type is not fulfilled in full here; the feast awaits the new creation, Revelation 19:9, and so the feeding is a first fruit, not the whole.

study.christ:
The woman puts the question of Jesus' identity into her first sentence: Lord, Son of David. A Canaanite who has never heard Him teach calls Him the descendant of Israel's king. She has understood that the promised ruler of David's line has power over demons and that His mercy is not a private possession. Matthew has already shown the blind making the same cry, Matthew 9:27, and will show it again at Jericho, Matthew 20:30 and 31. Here a Gentile makes it first.

Jesus' hard saying reveals His obedience. He was sent to the lost sheep of Israel, and He keeps to that mission with a discipline that no pressure moves, not even the pleas of a suffering mother. In this He is like the servant of Isaiah, who does exactly what the Father sends Him to do. Yet that same obedience is what opens the door: Paul says Christ became a servant to the circumcised in order to confirm the promises, so that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy, Romans 15:8 and 9. The order is not an obstacle but the road.

The feeding shows Him as the shepherd who provides in the wilderness. Matthew uses the word splanchnizomai, compassion, which in his Gospel marks Jesus' response to crowds who are harassed and helpless, Matthew 9:36. He does not wait for the disciples to bring a solution, and He does not dismiss the crowd. He takes the loaves, gives thanks, breaks and gives, a series of acts the church later saw reflected in the Lord's Supper, Matthew 26:26. The disciples hand out what He gives, so they are His channel and not His source.

There is a connection between the two panels that points to the cross. The woman asks for crumbs and is told by Jesus that her faith is great; the hungry are given more than enough. Both show that He can give without being diminished. Later He will give Himself, in a body broken for many, so that the nations may eat. The passage should not be turned into a tidy allegory in which each loaf stands for something. Its main weight is that He is the Messiah of Israel whose mercy is for all who come in faith.
study.god:
The passage reveals a God of ordered and overflowing grace. The order is real: He chose Israel, and the Messiah's earthly mission is addressed to Israel first. The overflow is also real, because that same election was for the sake of the nations, Genesis 12:3. The story refuses to choose between particularity and universality. It holds them together by showing that the Gentile woman comes in by the door Israel's own promises opened.

The God of this passage is attentive to persistence. The woman's repeated cries are not a nuisance to be managed but faith being formed. Scripture elsewhere teaches that God hears those who keep asking, Luke 18:1 to 8, and delights to hear a humble reply. He also delights in the faith itself: Jesus calls hers great, a rare word in the Gospels, used of the centurion in Matthew 8:10, and never of the disciples, who are often named 'of little faith'.

The feeding shows His compassion in concrete form. The crowd has been with Him three days and has nothing to eat, and Jesus says, I do not want to send them away hungry, verse 32. God cares about bodies, hunger and the road home. The doctrine of providence is thick with this, and so is the doctrine of the incarnation, since the Lord who feeds is a man who has known hunger, Matthew 4:2.

A tension is held without resolution: He is free to withhold, and He is generous. The silence of verse 23 is not indifference; it is the silence of One who intends to give. The tension is not explained, but it is resolved in the outcome. God's apparent delays in answering prayer may be part of a larger purpose, though we should not assume that every delay carries such a meaning.

For worship, the passage gives believers words to pray from the margins. The woman does not claim a seat at the table, only the crumbs, and finds that her Master's table is larger than she thought. It also leads the Gentile crowd to glorify the God of Israel, verse 31: the end of mercy is the praise of His name.

crossReferences.note: The earlier instruction to the twelve, not to go onto the road of the Gentiles but to the lost sheep of Israel. It explains what Jesus means in verse 24 and shows the mission order was consistent. The Great Commission later lifts the restriction, which makes the woman's story a hinge between the two.

The centurion's faith, another Gentile whom Jesus marveled at, saying He had found no one in Israel with such great faith. Together the two stories frame the Gospel's early view of the nations: many will come from east and west to the banquet of the kingdom, and faith, not ancestry, is the mark.

God sends Elijah to Zarephath of Sidon, to a widow He has commanded to provide for him. It shows that the coast where the Canaanite woman lived had already been a place of God's mercy, and that He had gone to a foreign woman in need long before Jesus came.

Jesus Himself cites the widow of Zarephath in Nazareth to show that God's favor is not held by Israel alone, and the crowd tries to throw Him off a cliff. The woman in Matthew 15 is the living example of what He said there.

The parallel account. Mark calls her a Greek of Syrophoenician origin, and has Jesus say 'First let the children have their fill', which stresses the order of the mission. It also places the healing of a deaf man in the Decapolis after her story, so the movement among the Gentiles is clearer.

The promise that foreigners who join themselves to the LORD will be brought to His holy mountain and that His house will be a house of prayer for all nations. The woman and the crowd on the mountain are early signs of this ingathering.

A banquet for all peoples on the LORD's mountain, where death is swallowed up. The feeding of the four thousand on a mountain, with the healed and the fed, is a preview, and the passage's mix of bread and healing matches the prophecy of food and the end of tears.

The LORD rains bread from heaven in the wilderness and tests Israel through it. The disciples' question about finding bread in a desolate place, verse 33, repeats Israel's own wilderness question, and Jesus answers it as the LORD did.

Elisha's feeding of a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, with some left over by the word of the LORD. It shows the Old Testament pattern of provision through a prophet that Jesus fulfills in His own person and on a far larger scale.

Jesus' own look back at the two feedings, naming the five loaves, the four thousand and the baskets gathered, as proof that the disciples should not worry about bread. It shows that the second feeding was meant to be remembered, and that failing to remember is itself a form of little faith.

Paul's summary of the order the woman met: Christ became a servant of the circumcised to confirm the promises to the patriarchs, so that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy. It reads like a commentary on verses 24 to 28.

The condition of Gentiles before Christ, separate and without hope, and then the change: brought near through His blood. The woman's story shows the first step of that nearness, and Paul shows what it finally cost.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a promise that blessing would come to all the families of the earth through one family, Genesis 12:3. Then, for most of the Old Testament, the focus is narrow: Israel is chosen, the Law is given to them, and the nations stand at the edge. Yet the edges are never sealed. Rahab, Ruth, Naaman, the widow of Zarephath and the sailors of Jonah's ship are all foreigners met by God, and the prophets look ahead to a day when the peoples will stream to the mountain of the LORD.

This passage stands where that long hope begins to move. Jesus lives out Israel's story in His own person, and so He first goes to the lost sheep. But the border yields as He crosses it, and a woman from the oldest enemy line of Canaan receives what Israel's children have. In the second panel He feeds crowds who give glory to the God of Israel, so that the stream toward the mountain is visible, if only as a trickle.

What the passage answers from before is the question of the nations: will the promise to Abraham ever reach them? Matthew says yes, and he says it through the faith of one woman and the compassion of one man. What it sets up is the Great Commission. When the risen Christ says to go and make disciples of all nations, Matthew 28:19, the order of verse 24 has run its course, and what Jesus began on the coast becomes the church's mission.

The story ends in the new creation with the feast the passage anticipates. Isaiah 25:6 sees a banquet for all peoples, and Revelation 7:9 describes a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language standing before the throne. In that crowd are the descendants of Tyre and Sidon, the ones once called dogs, fed at the table with the children. The bread that Jesus breaks on the mountain by the sea is the first course of that meal.

quiz.q: What was remarkable about the Canaanite woman?

options.text: As a Gentile she showed great, humble, persistent faith in Israel's Messiah.
options.note: Verses 22-28 highlight her faith, which Jesus calls great, despite every obstacle.

options.text: She was a Gentile who came to Jesus for help.
options.note: True and significant, but it omits the heart of the scene, the greatness of her faith.

options.text: She argued cleverly enough to change Jesus' mind against His will.
options.note: Her words are humble faith, not a debate that overpowers Jesus; He was drawing out her faith.

options.text: She demanded healing as something she deserved.
options.note: She claimed nothing as her due, only the crumbs of mercy, the opposite of demanding her rights.

quiz.q: What does Jesus' saying about the children's bread and the dogs reveal?

options.text: Salvation comes to Israel first, yet its abundance overflows to the Gentiles.
options.note: The image keeps Israel's priority while the woman rightly sees mercy spilling to the nations.

options.text: That Jesus cared only about the people of Israel.
options.note: He does state Israel's priority, but the scene ends with mercy reaching a Gentile, so this is too narrow.

options.text: That Gentiles were worthless in God's eyes.
options.note: Jesus uses the gentle word for a household pet and honors her faith; the point is order, not contempt.

options.text: That faith makes no difference to how Jesus responds.
options.note: Her faith is exactly what Jesus commends and rewards.

quiz.q: What moved Jesus to feed the four thousand?

options.text: Deep compassion for the hungry crowd who had been with Him three days.
options.note: Verse 32 says Jesus had compassion, unwilling to send them away faint.

options.text: A desire to prove His power with a miracle.
options.note: The feeding does display His power, but the stated motive is compassion, not display.

options.text: The disciples' request that He provide bread.
options.note: The disciples doubted it could be done; the initiative and compassion were Jesus'.

options.text: The crowd's demand that He feed them.
options.note: The crowd made no such demand; Jesus acted out of His own compassion.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the second feeding on the far shore?

options.text: Jesus' provision reaches toward the Gentiles, foreshadowing bread for all nations.
options.note: Placed after the Canaanite woman and toward Gentile territory, it signals the widening of mercy.

options.text: Jesus simply repeated an earlier miracle for a new crowd.
options.note: It is a real second feeding, but the placement and setting carry the added meaning of reaching the nations.

options.text: It shows the disciples had finally learned to trust Him fully.
options.note: The disciples again doubt there is enough bread, so this misreads their response.

options.text: It proves that Jesus fed only the people of Israel.
options.note: The setting leans toward Gentile ground, and the crowd glorifies the God of Israel as outsiders.

questions: The woman refused to give up when heaven seemed silent. Where do you need to keep bringing a request to Jesus even when the answer seems delayed?
She asked only for crumbs and received great mercy. How does approaching God in humility, rather than entitlement, change the way you pray?
Jesus called her faith great. What obstacle to faith, in your background, failures, or circumstances, is Jesus inviting you to press through to Him?
The same compassion that fed the crowd meets your needs. Where do you need to trust that Christ sees your hunger and will provide?
The gospel overflows every border. Who around you might feel like an outsider to God's mercy, and how could you carry the bread of Christ to them?

translationNotes.note: Canaanite is Matthew's deliberate archaic term for the woman's people, the ancient pagan inhabitants of the land, underscoring that she is a Gentile far outside the covenant.
The word rendered dogs is the diminutive for little household dogs or puppies, not wild scavengers; the gentler term is what the woman builds her humble reply upon.
The region of Magadan is otherwise unknown and appears as Magdala or Dalmanutha in some manuscripts and parallels; the exact location is uncertain but lay by the Sea of Galilee.
